clue.text: Force meeting with defeat — it's a very thin line?

parts.note: a loss is a defeat in a match or contest

explanation.surface: A force that ends up beaten is reduced to almost nothing, like a thin line on a map.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the definition by example: the thread is literally a fine line, not a battle line.
explanation.definitionFit: Floss is fine silk thread, such as the dental kind drawn between teeth, so a very slender strand.

clue.text: Decorative cape provided by some terrific husband

indicators.note: provided by some means only part of the following words supplies the letters

parts.note: the letters run across the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A wonderful husband has supplied a pretty wrap.
explanation.definitionFit: A fichu is a small triangular shawl worn round the shoulders, a decorative cape.

clue.text: Old friend stuck with nervous response of the eye

parts.note: O is a standard abbreviation for old

indicators.note: stuck with means having something lodged inside

parts.note: a pal is a friend
a tic is an involuntary twitch

explanation.surface: An old friend is stuck with an involuntary twitch of the eye.
explanation.walkthrough: The word for friend holds the twitch in its middle.
explanation.definitionFit: Optical means relating to sight or the eye.

clue.text: Startled, saying "Run" after incursion by Australian, bloodthirsty

indicators.note: an incursion is an invasion, so one letter gets inside the others
something startled is jolted out of place, so the letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
A is the abbreviation for Australian

explanation.surface: A frightened settler, crying 'Run!' after an Australian raid, describes the attackers as bloodthirsty.
explanation.definitionFit: Sanguinary means eager for bloodshed, from the Latin for blood.

clue.text: Unhappy Reginald, worried, losing head

indicators.note: a word losing its head has its first letter cut away

parts.note: Reg is the usual short form of the name Reginald
fretful means anxious or worried

explanation.surface: Poor anxious Reginald is unhappy and seems to be going bald.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Losing head' looks like Reginald's hair, but it applies to the word for worried, which drops its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone regretful feels sorrow over what happened, a close synonym for unhappy.

clue.text: Little space to hide, say, between manure and cesspit?

indicators.note: between asks only for what lies at the meeting point of the two words that follow, so the far ends of each are discarded

parts.note: taken as written; only its tail sits next to the gap
taken as written; only its head sits next to the gap

explanation.surface: A grim hiding place, squeezed between the dung heap and the sewage pit.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters straddle the gap between the two smelly words, skipping the 'and' that joins them.
explanation.definitionFit: A recess is a small alcove or niche, the sort of nook one might hide in.

clue.text: Target of jewellery raid left holding broken stem

indicators.note: something broken is in pieces, so the letters are reassembled differently
holding means keeping something inside

parts.note: someone who has left has gone
the letters of stem, rearranged

explanation.surface: Thieves raiding a jeweller's left, clutching a snapped stem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' looks like the opposite of right but means departed.
explanation.definitionFit: Gemstones are what thieves are after in a jewellery robbery, the precious stones themselves.

clue.text: Upset the writer receiving a poor mark in test

indicators.note: in a down clue, upset means turned upside down, so read from bottom to top
receiving means taking something in

parts.note: the writer of a clue refers to himself as me
taken as written
X is the cross marking a wrong answer

explanation.surface: The writer is upset after getting a bad mark in a test.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' applies to the whole assembly: the writer holding the article and the cross, then turned over.
explanation.definitionFit: An exam is a formal test of knowledge.

clue.text: Parisian idler displaying expensive coat around alley

indicators.note: around means encircling the following item

parts.note: a fur is a costly coat
a lane is a narrow alley

explanation.surface: A Paris loafer shows off a costly coat while strolling down an alley.
explanation.definitionFit: Flaneur is French for a stroller or idle man-about-town who wanders the streets observing.

clue.text: Computer arrangement a depressing affair for person of property

parts.note: a LAN is a local area network of computers
a downer is something dispiriting

explanation.surface: Setting up the computers proved a miserable business for the property owner.
explanation.definitionFit: A landowner is someone who owns land, a person of property.

clue.text: Abundant supply reduced and … what did you say?

parts.note: something reduced has been cut
taken as written
'come again?' is a colloquial way of asking someone to repeat themselves

explanation.surface: Someone hears the abundant supply has been cut and, startled, asks to have that repeated.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase originally described a joint of meat you could keep carving from, hence any plentiful source.
explanation.definitionFit: A cut-and-come-again is a plentiful source you can keep returning to, like a joint carved repeatedly.

clue.text: Quality of oil? Blasting of US county will secure it

indicators.note: to secure something is to hold it fast inside, so one piece wraps around another
blasting something blows it apart, so the place name is scattered into a new order

parts.note: the letters of these two words, to be rearranged
taken as written

explanation.surface: An oil industry piece: drilling explosions in an American county will lock in the find.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged letters of US county hold IT near the end. The question mark is there because the definition is literal rather than the usual figurative smarminess.
explanation.definitionFit: Unctuosity is oiliness, literally the greasy texture of oil as well as a smarmy manner.

clue.text: Andromeda's heart perhaps is for Perseus?

parts.note: something of Andromeda's is hers, the pronoun her

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its central letter

parts.note: the centre letter of this nine-letter name

explanation.surface: A myth: Andromeda gives her heart to Perseus, who saved her from the sea-monster.
explanation.walkthrough: The name works twice: as the owner, giving her, and as the word whose heart supplies a letter. Perseus is the classic hero who rescued Andromeda.
explanation.definitionFit: Perseus is an example of a mythological champion, the slayer of Medusa who rescued Andromeda.

clue.text: Likely to spread too, causing boils

indicators.note: something that boils churns about, so the letters are stirred into a new order

parts.note: the letters of these two words

explanation.surface: A doctor's warning that an infection may spread and bring on boils as well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boils' looks like a noun for skin eruptions, fitting the medical surface, but it is a verb signalling rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: A contagious disease passes readily from person to person, so it is liable to spread.

clue.text: Declining, not fine, sick

indicators.note: not here means leave out the following item from the word before it

parts.note: something failing is declining
F is the pencil-grade abbreviation for fine

explanation.surface: A medical bulletin: the patient is going downhill, not well, ill.
explanation.walkthrough: The three adjectives read as a list of symptoms; only the last is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone ailing is unwell, the same as being sick.

clue.text: Not using oxygen? Possibly be a con with air provided

indicators.note: possibly suggests one possible arrangement among many of the letters given

parts.note: the letters of these three words
taken as written

explanation.surface: Is it a fraud to claim something runs without oxygen when air is being supplied?
explanation.walkthrough: The fun is that air is in the fodder while the answer means doing without oxygen.
explanation.definitionFit: Anaerobic describes organisms or processes that function without oxygen, the opposite of aerobic.

clue.text: European and American openness not initially progressed

indicators.note: not initially means without its first letter

parts.note: candor is the American spelling of candour, frankness
ran, as a business or campaign progressed

explanation.surface: European and American frankness has failed to move forward from the start.
explanation.walkthrough: 'And' looks like part of the wordplay but just joins the definition; the AND in the answer comes from the American spelling of candour losing its C.
explanation.definitionFit: An Andorran is a native of Andorra, the small European principality in the Pyrenees.

clue.text: US comedian almost positioned close to the batter? Not I

indicators.note: almost means not quite complete, so the final letter is dropped
not here instructs leaving out the letter that follows

parts.note: something positioned has been set
the infield is the area near the batter in baseball or cricket
taken as written

explanation.surface: A comedian nearly placed in the field near the batter, but not me, says the player.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Batter' might suggest cooking but is the hitter in baseball or cricket. Jerry Seinfeld is the American stand-up behind the sitcom Seinfeld.
explanation.definitionFit: Jerry Seinfeld is a famous American stand-up comedian and sitcom star.

clue.text: Lawyer recalled cheers with university abandoning contest

indicators.note: something recalled is brought back, so the word is read in the other direction

parts.note: ta is British slang for thank you

indicators.note: abandoning means leaving out, so one letter is dropped from the next word

parts.note: a tourney is a tournament or contest
U is the standard abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: A lawyer remembers the cheering after a university pulled out of a competition.
explanation.walkthrough: Ta is everyday British slang for thanks, which 'cheers' also means.
explanation.definitionFit: An attorney is a lawyer, especially in American usage.

clue.text: Time without permanent employees captured in paint

parts.note: a business without permanent employees uses temps, temporary staff
an era is a period of time

explanation.surface: A period with no permanent staff, recorded in a painting.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole phrase reads as a description, an era of temps, with the staffing word placed first.
explanation.definitionFit: Tempera is a paint made by binding pigment with egg yolk, used by Renaissance painters.

clue.text: Finished going through spoils, returning in intoxicated state

indicators.note: going through places one piece inside another
returning means going back, so the word is read from the end

parts.note: food that spoils rots
time is up when it is finished

explanation.surface: Someone finished rifling through stolen loot comes home drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spoils' looks like a noun meaning loot but is the verb, to go bad.
explanation.definitionFit: A stupor is a dazed, near-unconscious condition, typically from drink.

clue.text: Makes enquiries mostly about tax relating to personal affairs

indicators.note: about means placed around the next item
mostly means not quite all, so the last letter goes

parts.note: someone who pries makes nosy enquiries
VAT is value added tax, a British sales tax

explanation.surface: Someone asks nosy questions about tax matters that are really their own business.
explanation.walkthrough: VAT is the UK's value added tax, charged on most goods and services.
explanation.definitionFit: Private means concerning one's personal life rather than public matters.

clue.text: Knowledge added to collection of animals after hauling up sea-monster

indicators.note: in a down clue, hauling up means the word is read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: Noah's ark held a collection of animals
ken means range of knowledge, as in beyond my ken

explanation.surface: Learning is gained about the animals after a sea-monster is hauled up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hauling up' fits a sea-monster being dragged from the deep, but it is the turnaround signal for Noah's vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: The kraken is a legendary giant sea-monster of Scandinavian folklore.

clue.text: Entertaining event: concert with piano at end

indicators.note: the word's letter for piano is moved to the final position

parts.note: a Prom is a promenade concert, as at the BBC Proms

explanation.surface: A fun evening out: a concert with a piano piece to finish.
explanation.walkthrough: P is the musical abbreviation for piano (quiet), and it moves from the front to the back. The Proms are a famous London summer concert series.
explanation.definitionFit: A romp is a lively, light-hearted entertainment such as a comic film or play.

clue.text: Cockney making suggestions about doctor, Unionist, having an affair

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so this word goes around the next pieces
a Cockney speaker drops the H at the start of words

parts.note: hinting is making suggestions
to doctor results is to rig them
U is the abbreviation for Unionist

explanation.surface: An East Ender drops hints about a doctor and a Unionist politician carrying on together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' looks like a noun such as DR or MO, but it is the verb meaning to tamper with. A Cockney is a working-class Londoner whose accent drops initial H.
explanation.definitionFit: Intriguing can mean carrying on a secret love affair, the old sense of an intrigue.

clue.text: Pistol exhibiting good safety mechanism

parts.note: G is a common abbreviation for good
a lock is a safety device

explanation.surface: A gun shown off with a reliable safety catch.
explanation.definitionFit: A Glock is an Austrian-made semi-automatic handgun.

clue.text: Plenty of water round here — I fish, saving nothing

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: saving here means except, so the fish's name is kept apart from the letter for nothing

parts.note: sole is a flatfish
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: An islander, surrounded by sea, says they go fishing but save none of the catch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saving' tempts as keeping, but here it means except, so the zero-shaped letter goes.
explanation.definitionFit: An isle is an island, land with sea all around it, so water in abundance on every side.

clue.text: Complains wood also filled with dull fruit

indicators.note: something filled with another thing holds it inside

parts.note: to beef is to grumble or complain
teak is a hardwood
too means also
mat (or matt) describes a dull, non-glossy finish

explanation.surface: Someone grumbles that the wood is also stuffed with dreary fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: The word for also is opened up to take the dull finish in its middle.
explanation.definitionFit: A beefsteak tomato is a large, meaty variety, and a tomato is botanically a fruit.

clue.text: University publisher family gathering about lecturer

indicators.note: gathering means drawing something in and enclosing it

parts.note: a clan is an extended family
re means concerning or about
a don is a university lecturer, especially at Oxford or Cambridge

explanation.surface: A university press hosts a family get-together around one of its lecturers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gathering' reads as a noun, a family gathering, but works as a verb enclosing the word for about.
explanation.definitionFit: The Clarendon Press is the imprint name of Oxford University Press, a famous academic publisher.

clue.text: Notorious logical figure having change of heart? Just a bit

indicators.note: a change of heart swaps the middle letter for a different one

parts.note: Mr Spock of Star Trek is famous for his cold logic

explanation.surface: A famously logical character has a change of heart, but only a little one.
explanation.walkthrough: The central O of the Star Trek Vulcan's name is replaced by E.
explanation.definitionFit: A speck is a tiny spot or particle, just a bit of something.
